Step 1: Understand the Word "Hollow" First

Before understanding the phrase, you need to understand the word "hollow".

Something is hollow when it is empty on the inside, even though it looks fine or solid from the outside.

Think of these examples:

  • A chocolate Easter egg is hollow — it has a shell, but nothing inside.
  • A bamboo stick is hollow — it has walls, but the center is empty air.
  • A dead tree trunk can become hollow — the inside rots away, leaving just the outer shell.

The key idea of "hollow" is: the outside looks okay, but the inside is missing or empty.

"Hollow out" is a phrasal verb. It means to make something hollow — that is, to remove or destroy the inside of something, leaving only the outer shell or surface.

It can be used in two major ways: literally and figuratively.

The literal meaning is physical and straightforward. It means to physically scoop out, dig out, or carve out the inside of an object.

Examples:

  • "She hollowed out a watermelon to use it as a bowl for fruit salad." — She scooped out the fruit from the inside, leaving the rind as a shell.
  • "They hollowed out a tree trunk to make a canoe." — They removed the wood from the inside, creating an empty boat shape.
  • "The thief hollowed out a book and hid the money inside it." — He cut out the pages from the inside, creating a secret hiding space.
  • "To make the dish, first hollow out the bell peppers and fill them with rice." — Remove the seeds and inner flesh of the peppers.

In all these cases, the outside stays intact, but the inside is deliberately removed to create empty space.
The Figurative Meaning (The More Important One)

This is where the phrase becomes truly powerful. "Hollow out" is used figuratively to describe a process where something is gradually weakened, drained, or emptied of its strength, meaning, value, or substance — even though it may still look the same from the outside.

Think of it like a tree that looks perfectly healthy from the outside, but has been eaten away from the inside by insects. It still stands, but it has no real strength left. One strong wind, and it will collapse.

This is exactly what "hollow out" means when used figuratively: something loses its inner substance, power, or core, even while the outer form still exists.

Figurative Example 1 — Institutions and Organizations

"Decades of corruption have hollowed out the country's justice system."

The courts still exist. The buildings are there. The judges still sit. But the system has been so corrupted from the inside that it no longer works properly. Its inner integrity — its core purpose — is gone.

"Budget cuts have hollowed out the country's public healthcare system."

Hospitals are still open, but there are not enough doctors, nurses, equipment, or medicine. The outer shell (the hospitals) remains, but the inner substance (the ability to actually care for people) has been stripped away.

Figurative Example 2 — The Economy and Jobs

One of the most common uses of "hollow out" in news and economics is describing the disappearance of certain types of jobs from society.

"Automation and technology have hollowed out the middle class."

This means that many middle-level jobs (like factory workers, clerks, and assembly line workers) have been replaced by machines. Only very high-skill jobs and very low-skill jobs remain. The "middle" — the core of the working economy — has been emptied out.

"Manufacturing in this region has been hollowed out over the past 30 years."

Factories closed. Jobs disappeared. The region still exists on a map, but the economic life inside it has been drained away.

Figurative Example 3 — Power, Authority, and Meaning

"The new regulations hollowed out the power of the local government."

The local government still exists and still has its name and offices. But all real decision-making power has been taken away from it. The form is there; the substance is not.

"Overuse has hollowed out the meaning of the word 'amazing'."

People use the word "amazing" to describe everything — their coffee, their socks, a mildly interesting video. Because it is used so carelessly, it has lost its true force and meaning. The word still exists, but its impact has been emptied out.

Figurative Example 4 — People and Emotions

"Hollow out" can also describe what happens to a person emotionally — when they feel deeply empty inside, usually after grief, trauma, or exhaustion.

"The loss of her child left her feeling completely hollowed out."

She is still alive. She still functions. But inside, she feels empty — like the grief has removed everything from her core.

"After months of overwork with no rest, he felt hollowed out — like there was nothing left inside him."

This describes total emotional and mental exhaustion, where a person has given so much of themselves that they feel like an empty shell.

In these cases, "hollowed out" is usually used as an adjective (describing the person's state) rather than an active verb.

"Hollow out" is a phrasal verb. Here is how it works:

1. As an active verb (someone/something does the hollowing):

  • "The company hollowed out its workforce." (The company removed most of its employees.)
  • "Years of neglect hollowed out the building."

2. In passive voice (something gets hollowed out by a force):

  • "The building was hollowed out by the fire."
  • "The middle class has been hollowed out by economic forces."

3. As an adjective (describing a state of being empty/drained):

  • "She felt hollowed out after the argument."
  • "The hollowed-out factory now stands as a reminder of the city's past."

4. The noun form — "hollowing out":

  • "The hollowing out of the middle class is a serious political issue."
  • "The hollowing out of traditional industries changed the region completely."
The Core Idea to Always Remember

No matter where you see "hollow out," the central idea is always the same:

The outer appearance or structure remains, but the inner substance, strength, or core has been removed or destroyed.

Whether it is a watermelon being physically scooped, a factory losing all its workers, a government losing its authority, a word losing its meaning, or a person losing their emotional energy — the pattern is always: shell stays, insides go.

To help you recognize the phrase in real life, here are the types of things most commonly described as being "hollowed out":

  • Institutions — governments, courts, schools, hospitals, churches
  • The economy — industries, sectors, the middle class, job markets
  • Organizations — companies, political parties, unions
  • People — someone feeling emotionally drained or empty
  • Words and concepts — when overuse makes a word lose its meaning
  • Communities — towns or regions that lose their population and economic life
  • Physical objects — fruit, vegetables, wood, books, shells

The key is always that the outer shape remains, but the inner substance is gone. It suggests a slow, gradual loss — not a sudden explosion, but a quiet emptying from within.
